To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the literature on meaningful change in QoL in oncology is inconsistent.
meaningful changes are not the same for all patients, but vary according to patient characteristics and the type of instrument used.

the most commonly used anchors for meaningful change in QoL instruments are performance status, overall QoL, and global rating of change; that the most common approach to determining meaningful change in QOL instruments is the distribution approach using standard deviations and standard errors of measurement; and that meaningful change for improvement is smaller than meaningful change for deterioration.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the question of what is considered a meaningful change for improvement and for deterioration in QoL.
the identification of a clinically meaningful change in oncological QoL instruments.
the identification and analysis of the most appropriate QoL measures and the determination of the magnitude of meaningful change in QoL measures for oncology patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
meaningful change in QoL instruments is not yet fully understood and further research is needed.
meaningful change in oncological QoL instruments is not yet fully understood and requires further investigation.
meaningful change is dependent on the QoL instrument used, the population studied and the direction of change.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a 0.3 standard deviation or a 5-point change on a 0.1–10 scale is a reasonable estimate of the minimum clinically important difference.

a meaningful change in QoL is 0.5–1.0 standard deviations for the EORTC QLQ-C30 and EORTC QoL QLQ-C15-PAL, 0.3–0.5 for the EORTQ QLQ-C29, 0.2–0.5 standard deviations for the FACT-G, and 0.3 standard deviation for the EORTCC QLQ-C19-PAL.
the literature is inconsistent on what constitutes a clinically meaningful change, but there are some consistent findings.
The main takeaway from our work is that
meaningful change should be determined in the target patient population.
the definition of a meaningful change in a given instrument should be based on the results of a validation study in the population of interest.
the concept of meaningful change in QoL is not a fixed entity, but a relative one.
